keys.label: Four keys

items.h: Arch Manning vs. the No. 131 pass defense
items.p: Florida allows 268.7 passing yards a game, which ESPN ranks 131st nationally, and 29.0 points a game (113th). Arch Manning is 92 of 146 for 1,122 yards, 10 touchdowns and five interceptions, and Texas averages 237.0 passing yards a game. Texas' own defense gives up 168.4 through the air.

items.h: Jadan Baugh and the run game vs. a Texas D that allows 96.0
items.p: Florida runs for 200.3 yards a game at 5.0 a carry, and Jadan Baugh has 110 carries for 672 yards and 12 touchdowns. Texas allows 96.0 rushing yards a game (ESPN rank 19th), 264.4 total yards (12th) and 16.0 points (21st). Texas runs for 142.2 at 3.7 a carry; Hollywood Smothers leads with 237 yards on 53 carries.

Florida is plus-3 in turnover margin with 10 takeaways and seven giveaways; Texas is plus-1 with eight and seven. Manning has thrown five interceptions, and Texas has taken 12 sacks in five games to Florida's eight in six. On defense Florida has 17 sacks, Jayden Woods leading with 4.5, and Texas has 18, Colin Simmons leading with 9.5.

Texas' defense has held opponents to 30.4% on third down (21 of 69); Florida's has allowed 46.2% (43 of 93). On offense the teams are close: Florida converts 45.2% (33 of 73) and Texas 44.6% (33 of 74).

lead.label: The Lead
lead.author: Franz Beard
lead.title: Philo's injury could give Tramell Jones Jr. his opening
lead.html:
It is unfortunate, but so often one man's injury is another man's opportunity. It was reported Wednesday that Florida (4-2, 2-2 SEC) starting quarterback Aaron Philo's availability is uncertain for Saturday's game in Austin against No. 7 Texas (4-1, 1-1 SEC). If Philo is unable to answer the bell against Texas (noon ET, ABC), Tramell Jones Jr. will be the starter.

Sumrall has said more than once that he believes the Gators can win with either Philo or Jones at quarterback, but certainly experience favors Philo, who has started all six games at UF including two on the road in SEC play (Auburn and Missouri).

Jones has played in seven games, all of them off the bench. His career stats are 44-for-64 passing (68.75 percent) for 443 yards (6.92 yards per attempt) with four touchdown passes and two interceptions. In his last two SEC games, Jones is 11-13 for 126 yards with one TD and one interception.

feature.label: The Big Picture
feature.author: Buddy Martin
feature.title: Is the SEC undergoing a drain of excellence?
feature.dek: Parody or parity? The SEC hasn’t lost excellence so much as its monopoly on it, and a 24-team playoff threatens to make the difference matter less.

image.alt: How the reported 24-team format would work: four Power 4 champions, the top Group of 6 team and 19 at-large teams, with seeds 1-8 getting a bye.

feature.caption: The reported 24-team format: four Power 4 champions, the top Group of 6 team and 19 at-large teams.
feature.html:
They have thrown out the bathwater and now they’re coming for the baby!

Apparently, there is nothing sacred left about college football, or the SEC.

That’s the way one side looks at it. The other side, led by the Matt Barries of the world, thinks we are in the throes of the “greatest football” weeks in history. Me, I worry that the scavengers have come for what’s left of college football.

As Nick Saban has said, it used to be more important for the Southern teams to win the SEC than the national championship. The preservation of that tradition seems more important than the money. But then there is this: ESPN reported that replacing the SEC championship game alone required accounting for an event generating roughly $80 million to $100 million.

I have generally found that when they say “it’s not about the money,” it is, indeed, about the money.

My take: The SEC hasn’t lost excellence. It has lost some of its monopoly on excellence, and a 24-team playoff threatens to make the distinction between “excellent” and “merely pretty good” matter less. Those are related problems, but they aren’t the same problem.
